guides.title: Confusion in the evening
guides.summary: When late afternoon and evening get harder

sections.heading: What is happening
items: Some people with dementia become more confused, restless or upset in the late afternoon or evening. This is often called sundowning.
Common triggers are being very tired, a body clock that is out of step, dim light and shadows, and picking up on a caregiver’s stress.

sections.heading: What to try right now
items: Come up to them calmly and gently. Speak softly.
Tell them they are safe and that you are there to help.
Do not argue or try to hold them back. If it is safe, let them pace.
Ask if they need something, such as the bathroom, a drink or a snack.
Make the room quiet and softly lit, with no dark corners. Turn off the TV and loud music. Play soothing music if they enjoy it.

sections.heading: What can help over time
items: Get outside, or sit by a window, in daylight every day.
Keep meals, bathing and bedtime at the same times each day.
Plan busier activities for the morning and early afternoon.
Limit long naps and dozing late in the day.
Avoid alcohol, caffeine and nicotine late in the day.

sections.heading: When to get help
items: Talk to a doctor about sleep problems. Treatable causes, such as a urinary tract infection or sleep apnea, can make things worse.

sources.name: National Institute on Aging
sources.title: Coping With Agitation, Aggression, and Sundowning in Alzheimer’s Disease

guides.title: Wandering
guides.summary: Staying safe if someone leaves or gets lost

urgent.title: If someone is missing right now
urgent.text: Start looking right away, beginning close to home. If you do not find them within 15 minutes, call 911 and say the person has dementia.

sections.heading: What is happening
items: Wandering is when a person walks away without a clear purpose, or keeps trying to “go home” when they are already home. It can be dangerous, because they can get lost or hurt.

sections.heading: Signs it may happen
items: Coming back late from walks or drives
Forgetting the way to familiar places
Saying they want to “go home” when they are home
Pacing, restlessness, or trouble finding the bathroom or bedroom
Seeming lost in a new or changed place

sections.heading: If they go missing
items: Start looking right away. Check close to home first.
If they are not found within 15 minutes, call 911.
Tell the operator that the person has dementia.
Give the police a recent, close-up photo.

sections.heading: Getting ready ahead of time
items: Keep a recent, close-up photo of them where you can find it fast.
Put bells above doors, or use a door monitor that signals when a door opens.
Make sure they carry ID, or wear a bracelet with their name and your phone number.
Ask about a wandering response service in your area.

sources.name: National Institute on Aging
sources.title: Coping With Alzheimer’s Behaviors: Wandering and Getting Lost

guides.title: Repeated questions
guides.summary: When the same question comes up again and again

sections.heading: What is happening
items: A person with dementia may ask the same question many times. They may not remember asking. The question can also be a way of saying they feel worried, bored or unsure.

sections.heading: What to try
items: Stay calm and patient. Use a gentle voice and touch.
Answer the question, even if you have to answer it several times.
Respond to the feeling. For example, “It sounds like you are worried. I am here.”
If they can still read, write the answer down and put it where they can see it. Clocks, calendars and photos can help too.
Offer something to do. They may be bored.

sections.heading: What can help over time
items: Look for a pattern: a time of day, a place, or certain people.
Keep a regular routine with pleasant activities.
If the repeating does no harm, it is okay to let it be.

sections.heading: Please avoid
items: Arguing or trying to use logic.
Saying “I already told you.” They cannot remember asking.

sources.name: National Institute on Aging
sources.title: Communicating With Someone Who Has Alzheimer’s Disease

guides.title: Anger and agitation
guides.summary: When someone is restless, upset or lashes out

urgent.title: If anyone is in danger
urgent.text: Call 911. Tell the operator that the person has dementia.

sections.heading: What is happening
items: Agitation means a person is restless and worried and cannot settle. They may pace, shout or lash out. There is usually a reason, even when it is hard to see.

Common causes include pain, an infection, hunger or thirst, tiredness, side effects of medicine, too much noise or too many people, feeling lost, being asked too many questions, and a sudden change in routine. They can also pick up on a caregiver’s stress.

sections.heading: What to try right now
items: Stay calm. Speak softly and keep your face and body relaxed.
Do not argue. Listen, and tell them they are safe.
Lower the noise and move away from crowds.
Think about what happened just before it started.
Check for pain, hunger, thirst or needing the bathroom.
Offer something calming, such as music, a snack, a walk or a simple chore together.
If it is safe, step away for a moment and take a breath.

sections.heading: Keep everyone safe
items: Lock up car keys and anything that could cause harm, such as guns and kitchen knives.

sections.heading: When to get help
items: See a doctor for a full checkup, especially if the change came on suddenly. Pain, infection and medicine side effects can all cause agitation.

sources.name: National Institute on Aging
sources.title: Coping With Agitation, Aggression, and Sundowning in Alzheimer’s Disease

guides.title: Everyday conversation
guides.summary: Ways to talk that lower stress for both of you

sections.heading: How to talk together
items: Go to them, make eye contact, and say their name.
Speak slowly and clearly, in a calm voice.
Use short, simple sentences. Say one thing at a time.
Ask yes or no questions. “Would you like some tea?” works better than “What would you like to drink?”
Give them time to answer. Try not to interrupt.
If they do not understand, try different words instead of repeating the same ones.
Talk in a quiet place with few distractions.

sections.heading: Your tone matters
items: Be aware of your tone, face and body language. Try to look relaxed and warm.
Be patient and try not to show frustration.

sections.heading: Please avoid
items: Arguing or correcting them.
Talking about them as if they are not in the room.
Baby talk or a baby voice.
